item.title: The question dominating Indian politics: Is it worse when women swear?
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy0zn6gy7zjo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
The question dominating Indian politics: Is it worse when women swear? - Published Recent footage of young women swearing during a protest in India has sparked an unusual debate: are expletives worse when they come from women? The latest to weigh in has been opposition MP Rahul Gandhi who criticised Prime Minister Narendra Modi's description of seeing young women swearing as a "culture shock". "If boys swear, there is no problem and it is allowed. But if a girl swears, it is a cultural shock," Gandhi said. The protesters had been directing their anger at the government and some of the foul language targeted the prime minister, leading to outrage among his supporters, with even many critics of Modi's politics saying the women had crossed a line. The protests ended a month ago, but Rahul Gandhi's remarks have renewed the debate over how female activism, women voicing their views, stridently - even with expletives - are viewed in the country. It started last month when some young women used foul language against the prime minister during the weeks-long Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protests in Delhi and other cities, seeking education reforms. Modi himself addressed the issue in a selfie video where he said it was "a culture shock" to see young women using expletives, but added that he forgave them. The prime minister, however, did not comment on the violent police crackdown against the protesters or support women who said they had been trolled and had received rape threats for attending the CJP protests. At the weekend, Rahul Gandhi, who serves as the leader of the opposition in the lower house of the Indian parliament, criticised Modi's "culture shock" comment at a gathering of students in the western city of Pune. Pointing out that both male and female protesters had used foul language during the protest over exam paper leaks, he asked why was Modi only talking about women? His comments came weeks after posters and videos of female protesters insulting Modi went viral on social media. As police opened an investigation into abusive posts, a 15-year-old girl became caught up in the centre of the controversy, with trolls sending her abuses and threats on social media. The teenager put out a video apologising for her language and seeking forgiveness. She also said that she had taken down her video, but the outrage continued. Her mother, a single parent, told the local press that the controversy had forced them to move home a number of times. Modi had been more conciliatory in his vertical video shared on Instagram after the protest had ended. "Some naughty children used extremely abusive expletives which have no place in a civilised society," he said. "They abused me, they also abused my late mother. It was deeply disturbing." Addressing the outrage from his supporters, he said he understood their anger. "It's a culture shock. How can our daughters use such language? But I want to say that mistakes are made in childhood and it's an opportunity to fix them." At the Pune event, Gandhi said Modi's singling out the gender of protesters was rooted in patriarchy. "What is the mindset that a girl has a place while boys get full freedom? They can do whatever they want, if they want to swear, they can swear... We have to smash this patriarchy," he said. Journalist Namita Bhandare who writes a popular column on gender issues in the Hindustan Times newspaper told the BBC that contrary to what people say, many "women in India of course swear, it's not new". In many villages of northern Indian, an important wedding ritual involves women from bride's family singing a medley of expletives while welcoming the groom's party - a tradition that nobody finds offensive. So, Bhandare says, describing what was said at Jantar Mantar as culture shock and calling women out for using swear words shows "double standards" because politicians of all hues, including the prime minister, have used slurs against women when it suited them. In his Independence Day speech in 2022, Modi called on Indians to fight misogyny. His government runs a number of scheme aimed at uplifting women and Modi enjoys tremendous popularity among female voters. But on many instances, Modi and his party colleagues have been criticised for being disrespectful to women. A number of senior party leaders have been called out for misogynistic comments about women's clothing. Modi himself has invited criticism for using terms such as "Jersey cow" in a 2004 rally and "50 crore ki girlfriend" ["girlfriend worth 500m rupee"] in another event in 2012. Such criticism is not confined to the BJP. Many opposition politicians, including those from Gandhi's Congress party, have also faced similar allegations. A Congress leader in Kerala state recently sparked outrage, external with remarks about using women to make false complaints against political opponents. "Women are treated so shabbily and it's so easy to target them. And then when they use profanity, then everyone asks, how can our girls cuss and swear," says Bhandare. Social activist Sunil Jalan, who's been running a Gali Bandh Abhiyan (a campaign aimed at stopping use of cuss words) since 2014, says "we must focus on swearing, not on the gender of who uses them". In a survey by his NGO last year, 55% of the more than 70,000 participants from across 28 Indian states and eight federally-administered territories admitted to using foul language. The question asked was straightforward: how often do you hear or use expletives that target mothers, sisters or daughters? Their 2025 Gali [expletive] Map of India showed very high prevalence rates in the north - 80% in Delhi, 78% in Punjab and 74% in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar states. Most southern states were below 44% and it was between 15% and 18% in the north-east. Jalan says this is the first time in the country that a dialogue over foul language is taking place, "and hopefully something good will come out of it". "It's a very serious issue. It's a virus that's spread through society. Comedy, jokes and films have normalised swearing and it needs to be reined in," he says. But many of India's Gen Z do not see profanity in the same way. "Profanity and protest have gone hand in hand for ages. There's a shock-and-awe factor to it, which is fundamental to protest," CJP spokesperson Sourav Das told the BBC earlier. "It may be distasteful to some people and not to others. But it absolutely can't be criminal." And such language is hardly confined to street protests. Profanity and personal attacks have increasingly become part of India's public discourse, from television debates to courtrooms and even parliament. A video that went viral earlier this week showed a female presenter on Indian government-owned Doordarshan channel trying to control a temple priest who let out a volley of cuss words at a Congress party spokesman who then retaliated in the same language. In 2023, BJP MP Ramesh Bidhuri was extensively criticised, external for using Islamophobic slurs against a Muslim MP and threatening him in Parliament. As outrage grew, he later said he regretted his statement. Sociologist Shiv Vishwanathan says "the use of expletives is the symptom of a deeper breakdown of democracy, it shows there's end of discussion and a lack of respect". When expletives are used inside Parliament and courts, he says, "it shows there's a breakdown of language, there's a decline of argument and decline of democracy". The use of profanity by protesters is because "when there's a weaker sense of respect, expletives become a response".

item.title: Canada's retaliation tests the limit of American power under Trump
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ce8xd5k1krpo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Canada's retaliation tests the limit of American power under Trump - Published Two days before US-Canada trade talks dramatically derailed, Vice-President JD Vance was telling an audience at a private fundraiser that Prime Minister Mark Carney was a "very sweet guy". In a private audio recording leaked to the Canadian Press, Vance reportedly went on to say that Carney "comes in and puffs his chest out and says: 'I'm going to, like, out-tough Donald Trump.'" He described that approach as "hilarious" because the Canadians ultimately "climb down on a lot of issues". Maybe those comments, which received considerable coverage in Canada, were not the proximate cause for Carney's diplomats to pack up and go home over the weekend. But they certainly didn't help. Carney's move abruptly terminated negotiations over a new trade agreement and sparked a fresh round of tariffs between neighbours who conduct more than $872bn (£640bn) in bilateral annual trade. The serious and deepening rift - and Vance's comments - offer the latest example of a Trump administration willing to exert force on the global stage against friend and foe alike, again highlighting the potentially disruptive consequences of such actions. What's more, if Trump thought the Canadians would cave in the face of American pressure - as many US allies have done over the past 19 months - he may have miscalculated. And the consequences of that mistake could linger for the rest of his presidency. Why is Trump targeting Canada? While the latest rupture is striking, friction between the US and Canada dates back to the first Trump administration and the negotiations that created the USMCA: the deal replacing the 1990s-era North American Free Trade Agreement (Nafta). Complicating matters were personal clashes between Trump and Justin Trudeau, who was then Canada's prime minister. As Trump prepared to return to the White House in late 2024, he derisively referred to Trudeau as "governor" and to Canada as America's "51st State." Underlying those insults was a geopolitical outlook that positioned the US primarily as a hemispheric power entitled to exert political, military, and economic influence over its immediate region – and that most definitely included Canada. Administration officials viewed Canada as contributing too little to regional defence while disproportionately benefiting from trade with its southern neighbour. In Trump's worldview, where economic security and national security are inextricably linked, Canada and Mexico - two of America's largest trading partners - became early, obvious targets. - Canada announces 'dollar-for-dollar' retaliatory tariffs - Published1 day ago - 'Half my business will be gone' - firms in Canada and US fear trade war - Published2 days ago - How Canada could hit back to hurt the US economy - and Trump - Published2 days ago It's why the US president said he wanted to take over Greenland too. "If you listen to really anybody in state, treasury, or commerce [departments], you will hear the phrase 'economic security is national security'," said Drew DeLong, head of corporate statecraft at the Kearney Foresight think tank. By the start of this year, however, as North American trade negotiations proceeded in fits and starts, Trump's attention shifted away from Canada to his military interventions in Venezuela and then the Middle East. Across every region, though, the core line of Trump's international strategy remains consistent: the US is a dominant power capable of imposing its will for national benefit. Trump's power tested by Canada - and Iran But power has limits. Trump's second term has been a continuous test of those limits - and, at times, a lesson in finding exactly where they are. While obvious differences exist between a shooting war in Iran and a trade dispute with Canada, the lessons are not dissimilar. In both, the US faces a counterpart that, despite having far less overall power, retains the means to retaliate. For Iran, that leverage lies in targeting US allies and disrupting global commerce by threatening maritime chokepoints like the Strait of Hormuz. Canada, for its part, is beginning to test its own ability to inflict economic pain. Tuesday's targeted tariffs mark a first step. Future measures could include restricting US access to Canadian energy and critical minerals, alongside consumer boycotts of American goods. "As the broader world shifts into a more economic security theatre, you see this game of chokepoints and leverage angles continue to pan out across supply chains," said DeLong. Countries just have to look for them, he added. For the moment, clear exit ramps are scarce. Trump has escalated his rhetoric, repeatedly accusing Canada of "ripping off" the US, while Ontario Premier Doug Ford fired back by telling the American president to "kiss my ass". "Every time we push allies and partners away, I think we incentivise them to look for new relationships and new partnerships rather than trying to acquiesce to US demands," said Imran Bayoumi, deputy director of the GeoStrategy Initiative at the Atlantic Council. Still, room remains for cooler heads to prevail. Canada's new tariffs take effect in two weeks, while the most significant US retaliation - a 50% tariff on Canadian-built vehicles and auto parts - will not kick in until early 2027. As with any conflict - economic or military - a cycle of escalation can prove difficult to break. However, the multi-month buffer before the next wave of US tariffs gives negotiators space to restart talks. Until Friday night, these had been showing some progress. A dilemma for Carney and Canada A more pressing deadline is November's US midterm elections. Democratic congressional victories could significantly curtail Trump's authority - or unexpected Republican success could embolden him further. At present, Ottawa seems content to bet on the former outcome, calculating that fear of a midterm blowout in key industrial battlegrounds like Michigan and Ohio will force Trump to back down before ballots are cast. "I don't think there's the kind of internal political divisions in Canada that maybe the Trump administration would have expected," Bayoumi said. "I think Carney has a lot of political runway to really get a good deal for Canada and not settle for anything less." There is another possibility that Carney has aired publicly since Trump returned to office, however. Canada may continue shifting away from the US altogether, charting a course that deliberately widens the distance between the two nations. As Carney noted: "We cannot depend on traditional alliances when the rules of the game have fundamentally changed." While geographic proximity ensures the two countries will remain intertwined, the deeply integrated economic relationship of recent decades may be coming to an end. In that respect, Canada presents a contrast with Mexico, which appears to be opting for even closer economic integration with the US. Meanwhile, other global trading partners - including US allies in Europe and Asia - are watching Canada's "elbows up" resistance as a plausible blueprint for future dealings with Trump. "Ten years from now, this is going to be taught in classrooms," said DeLong. "You have these bifurcating paths within North America, and the question is: Are they going to come back together, or is this going to continue to split? And if it does, who benefits most in the long run?" If the supposedly easygoing Canadians can stand up to their pugnacious – and powerful - neighbour, others may decide they can, too.

Moment tornado tears through southern France A destructive tornado has torn through villages in southern France, injuring more than 40 people. An eyewitness from the village of Verzeille recorded the tornado forming beneath a thunderstorm. Winds of more than 100km/h (62mph) ripped the roofs off homes in Pomas. Local authorities say about 2,800 households were still without electricity on Monday evening, while several roads were blocked. Watch: Moment humanoid robot beats Usain Bolt's 100m record A robot has outperformed humans by running faster than Usain Bolt's 100m sprint world record at the World Humanoid Robot Games in China. The humanoid robot, developed by the Beijing Innovation Centre of Humanoid Robotics, ran the distance in 9.39 seconds at the event. Eight-time Olympic gold medallist Bolt set the world record for humans in 2009, running 100m in 9.58 seconds. The robot beat two others including one made by Chinese smartphone maker Honor - which the manufacturer says ran the distance in 9.32 seconds in a test run. Other events at the robot games, which started on Saturday, include boxing and football, but also household tasks such as folding laundry. The BBC's China correspondent Laura Bicker reports from Beijing.
